etymology: Hebrew yotbathah, “goodness” or “pleasantness,” a station of Israel in the wilderness, remembered by Moses as a land of rivers of waters.
biblical_def: Jotbathah was a station in the wilderness wanderings of Israel, set down in the careful register of their journeyings which the LORD commanded Moses to write (Num 33:33). When Moses recounted the way unto the people, he marked it especially as “a land of rivers of waters” (Deu 10:7), a green and gracious resting-place amid the dry and thirsty land where no water is. The name itself signifies “goodness” or “pleasantness,” and the providence of God answered to the name, for He led His people to streams in the desert as a token of His tender care over them. The dictionary marks that the LORD who brought them through the great and terrible wilderness did not leave them to perish of thirst, but appointed waters for them at Jotbathah as surely as He had appointed the cloud by day and the fire by night. There is a figure here of Him who is the fountain of living waters, the Lord Jesus Christ, who cries, If any man thirst, let him come unto Me and drink. Jotbathah stands as a witness that the journey of the church through this world is measured mile by mile by a faithful God, who plants His pilgrims beside rivers of water and brings them at the last unto the land where the goodly heritage is theirs for ever.

etymology: Hebrew ‘abronah, perhaps “passage” or “crossing-place,” a station of Israel in the wilderness near the gulf of the Red Sea.
biblical_def: Ebronah was a station in the wilderness wanderings of Israel, named in the register of their journeyings between Jotbathah and Ezion-geber as the people drew near the gulf of the Red Sea (Num 33:34). Of the place itself the Scripture records nothing beyond its name and its position in the line of march, yet that is no small thing, for the Spirit of God thought it good to set down every encampment of His people in the holy book. The name perhaps signifies “passage” or “crossing-place,” fitting for a station hard by the arm of the sea. The dictionary does not invent a history where Scripture is silent; it honours that the LORD numbered each resting-place of Israel as a shepherd numbers the steps of his flock. These obscure names are the milestones of a great deliverance, the record of a God who went before His people in all the way that they went. There is comfort here for the wayfaring saint, that not a single stage of the pilgrimage is forgotten of the LORD, neither the famous places of miracle nor the nameless camps remembered by a single word. Ebronah stands as a witness that He who appointed the bounds of habitation appointed also the path of His redeemed, and keeps the reckoning of every mile until His people come unto their rest.

etymology: Hebrew ‘etsyon geber, “backbone of a man” or “spine of the giant,” a station of Israel and afterward a port upon the Red Sea where Solomon built his navy.
biblical_def: Ezion-geber was a station in the wilderness wanderings of Israel, encamped beside the Red Sea, and afterward a haven of great note in the kingdom of Israel (Num 33:35). When the people turned to compass the land of Edom, they passed by the way of the plain from Elath and from Ezion-geber, the LORD leading them along the arm of the sea (Deu 2:8). In the days of the kingdom this port became the harbour whence King Solomon launched his navy, which fetched gold from Ophir for the house of the LORD (1Ki 9:26). Thus a nameless camp of the wanderings became in the providence of God a gate of nations and a treasury of the temple’s gold. The dictionary marks how the LORD made the place of His people’s pilgrimage to serve His purpose in after generations, so that the same shore where the weary tribes pitched their tents bore the ships of the wise king. There is a figure here of the wisdom of God, who orders the smallest stage of the desert march toward ends His people could not see. Ezion-geber stands as a witness that nothing in the journey of the church is wasted, but that the very ground of our pilgrimage the LORD takes up into His great design, until the gold of the nations is brought home to the house of God.

etymology: Hebrew tsalmonah, “shady” or “place of the image,” a station of Israel in the wilderness, in the region where the brazen serpent was lifted up.
biblical_def: Zalmonah was a station in the wilderness wanderings of Israel, named in the register of their journeyings after they departed from mount Hor (Num 33:41). It lay in the region where the people, journeying from mount Hor to compass the land of Edom, grew discouraged because of the way, and spake against God and against Moses, and the LORD sent fiery serpents among them (Num 21:4). When the bitten were dying, Moses by the LORD’s command made a serpent of brass and set it upon a pole, that whosoever looked upon it might live. The name Zalmonah signifies “shady” or, by another reading, “place of the image,” which some have linked to that very brazen serpent. The dictionary honours the station as a marker of one of the great types of the gospel, for the Lord Jesus said, As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up, that whosoever believeth in Him should not perish. Zalmonah stands therefore in the very country of grace, where the bitten and dying were healed by a look of faith. It is a witness that in the place of our murmuring and our death the LORD set up His remedy, and that the lifted-up Christ is life to all who turn their eyes to Him.

etymology: Hebrew ’oboth, “water-skins” or “bottles,” a station of Israel in the wilderness as they journeyed toward the border of Moab.
biblical_def: Oboth was a station in the wilderness wanderings of Israel, named in the register of their journeyings as they drew near the end of the long march toward the plains of Moab (Num 33:43). After Zalmonah and Punon the people pitched in Oboth, and from thence they removed and pitched in Ije-abarim, in the wilderness which is before Moab toward the sunrising (Num 21:10). The name perhaps signifies “water-skins” or “bottles,” the leathern vessels in which the wayfarer carried his water through the dry land, a name fitting for a people sustained mile by mile by the daily mercy of God. Of the place itself the Scripture records little beyond its station in the line of march, yet it is a milestone of the homeward way, for here the wanderings of forty years were drawing toward their close, and the borders of the promised inheritance came at last in sight. The dictionary honours that the LORD brought His people through unto this near approach, neither abandoning them in the wilderness nor suffering the journey to fail short of its end. Oboth stands as a witness that the God who began the deliverance at the Red Sea will finish it at the river Jordan, and that the pilgrim who has come so far may trust the faithful LORD to bring him home to the goodly heritage He has promised.

etymology: Hebrew ‘iyye ha-‘abarim, “ruins of the regions beyond” or “heaps of the passes,” a station of Israel in the border of Moab, called also Iim.
biblical_def: Ije-abarim was a station in the wilderness wanderings of Israel, pitched in the border of Moab as the people came near the end of their long journeying (Num 33:44). It is named also simply Iim, and it lay in the wilderness which is before Moab toward the sunrising, hard by the territory of the Abarim, the regions beyond the Jordan from which Moses should at the last behold the promised land (Num 21:11). The name signifies “ruins of the regions beyond” or “heaps of the passes,” and it marks the threshold of the inheritance, where the wilderness gives way to the borders of Moab and the plains where Israel should muster before the crossing. The dictionary honours that the LORD brought His pilgrim people unto the very edge of the land He had sworn to their fathers, that the wanderings might be exchanged for the conquest and the rest. There is a figure here of the believer’s last stage, who comes through the wilderness of this world unto the borders of the better country, and stands within sight of the city which hath foundations. Ije-abarim stands as a witness that the LORD who led His people out of Egypt led them also unto the threshold of Canaan, and that He who has begun a good work in His own will perform it until the day when they pass over into the inheritance prepared for them.

etymology: Hebrew dibon gad, “wasting” or “pining” of Gad, a station of Israel beyond Jordan, afterward a city built by the children of Gad.
biblical_def: Dibon-gad was a station in the wilderness wanderings of Israel, pitched beyond the river Jordan as the people drew toward the plains of Moab (Num 33:45). It is named Dibon-gad, that is, the Dibon of the tribe of Gad, for when the land east of Jordan was given to Reuben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, the children of Gad built Dibon and Ataroth and Aroer and the other cities of that goodly country for cattle (Num 32:34). Thus a station of the wandering became a settled inheritance, and the name of the tribe was joined for ever to the place they builded. The dictionary marks how the LORD, who led His people through the trackless waste, gave to them at the last cities to dwell in and fields for their flocks, fulfilling the word of His promise to their fathers. There is a witness here of the goodness of God, who does not leave His people in the wilderness but brings them into a wide and settled rest. Dibon-gad stands as a token that the journey has its end in inheritance, and that the same providence which appointed the bounds of the people’s habitation gave to each tribe its portion. He who brought Gad through the desert planted Gad in the land, and the believer’s pilgrimage too shall end in the rest the LORD has prepared.

etymology: Hebrew ‘almon diblathaymah, perhaps “hiding-place of the two cakes of figs,” a station of Israel beyond Jordan near the mountains of Abarim.
biblical_def: Almon-diblathaim was a station in the wilderness wanderings of Israel, pitched beyond Jordan as the people drew toward the close of their long journeying, between Dibon-gad and the mountains of Abarim before Nebo (Num 33:46). From thence they removed and pitched in the mountains of Abarim, and after that came down into the plains of Moab by Jordan near Jericho, where the whole host should muster before the crossing (Num 33:47). The name perhaps signifies “hiding-place of the two cakes of figs,” a fruitful and homely name speaking of provision in the wilderness. Of the place itself Scripture records little more than its station in the line of march, yet it is one of the last camps before the Abarim, from whose heights Moses should behold the promised land. The dictionary honours that the LORD set down even this near and nameless station, for every encampment of His people was numbered in His book. There is comfort here for the saint near the end of his course, that the LORD forgets not the final stages of the way. Almon-diblathaim stands as a witness that He who led His people through forty years brought them safely unto the last camps before the inheritance, and that the God who keeps the reckoning of every mile will bring His own at the last unto the rest He has prepared.

etymology: Hebrew lod, perhaps “travail” or “strife,” a town built by the Benjamites, resettled by the returning captivity, and known in the New Testament as Lydda.
biblical_def: Lod was a town first builded by the sons of Elpaal of the tribe of Benjamin, who builded Ono and Lod, with the towns thereof (1Ch 8:12). After the long captivity in Babylon the men of Lod were numbered among those who returned with Zerubbabel to dwell again in the land of their fathers (Ezr 2:33), and Lod with its towns is named among the places where the children of Benjamin settled after the return (Neh 11:35). In the days of the New Testament the town was called Lydda, and there the apostle Peter came down to the saints and healed Aeneas, who had kept his bed eight years sick of the palsy, saying, Aeneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole; and all that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him, and turned to the Lord (Act 9:34). The dictionary marks how the LORD kept this one town through the centuries, from the building of the Benjamites, through the ruin of the captivity, unto the resettling of the remnant, and at the last made it a place where the gospel was preached and a whole region turned to Christ. Lod stands as a witness to the faithfulness of God over the long generations, who plants a people, and brings them home from exile, and visits them in the fulness of time with the salvation of His Son.

etymology: Hebrew ’ono, “vigorous” or “strong,” a town built by the Benjamites, in the plain of Ono, resettled after the captivity.
biblical_def: Ono was a town builded by the sons of Elpaal of the tribe of Benjamin, who builded Ono and Lod, with the towns thereof (1Ch 8:12). Its men returned from the captivity of Babylon with Zerubbabel, the children of Lod, Hadid, and Ono being numbered among the remnant that came again to the land (Ezr 2:33), and it is named with Lod among the dwelling-places of Benjamin in the valley of craftsmen after the return (Neh 11:35). In the days of Nehemiah, when the wall of Jerusalem was building, the adversaries Sanballat and Geshem sent unto him, saying, Come, let us meet together in some one of the villages in the plain of Ono; but they thought to do him mischief, and Nehemiah answered, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down (Neh 6:2). Thus the plain of Ono became the scene of a faithful servant’s steadfastness, who would not leave the LORD’s work to parley with His enemies. The dictionary honours that the LORD kept this Benjamite town through building, exile, and return, and made its plain a witness to holy resolution. Ono stands as a token that the providence of God preserves the places and the people of His promise, and that the servant set to a great work must not come down from it at the bidding of them that seek his hurt.
